name: Research datasets of font impressions: O'Donovan 2014 attributes, FontLex 2018, Shaikh personality studies (2006, 2016), the MyFonts tag dataset (Chen et al. 2019) and its co-occurrence embeddings
what_it_is: Four families of human impression data, and what each concretely is. (1) O'Donovan, Libeks, Agarwala, Hertzmann 2014 (ACM TOG 33(4), SIGGRAPH): 200 fonts rated by crowd workers on 31 relative attributes (thin, strong, wide, soft, disorderly, artistic, complex, playful, calm, dramatic, sloppy, clumsy, bad, attention-grabbing, formal, attractive, legible, charming, gentle, modern, pretentious, happy, graceful, fresh, friendly, delicate, warm, technical, angular, boring, sharp), each scaled 0 to 100 from pairwise 'which is more X' answers (Bradley-Terry with rater reliability), plus 6 hand-labelled binary attributes (capitals, cursive, display, italic, monospace, serif). That is the '37 attributes'. The crowd labels exist only for 200 fonts; a gradient-boosted-tree model trained on them then predicts all 37 for the full 1,278-font set (1,138 Google Web Fonts plus web fonts seen on about 3,800 design-oriented pages seeded from the Typekit blog). Downloads on the project page: attribute.zip, similarity.zip (with Matlab metric-learning code), gwfonts.zip. (2) FontLex (Kulahcioglu and de Melo, LREC 2018): a lexicon linking 6,721 words to the same 200 O'Donovan fonts (200-dimensional word vectors) through ten emotion attributes (the NRC set: anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, negative, positive, sadness, surprise, trust) and word-emotion links, extended with WordNet synonyms of the attribute names. Not 2,000 fonts: the abstract says 6.7K words and 200 fonts. A companion paper (Predicting Semantic Signatures of Fonts, 2018) predicts attribute scores for unseen fonts as the weighted average of the nearest four fonts in CNN-embedding space, with about 9% mean absolute error by leave-one-out. (3) Shaikh, Chaparro and Fox 2006 (Usability News 8(1)): 561 participants rated 20 fonts on 15 adjective pairs (4-point scale) and chose appropriate uses from 25; factor analysis grouped the fonts into five families (serif, sans serif, modern display, script/funny, monospace). The 'Activity' factor comes from the later book chapter (Shaikh and Chaparro, Digital Fonts and Reading, 2016): 40 typefaces, 15 semantic-differential scales, three correlated factors named Potency (ruggedness, masculinity), Evaluative (beauty, value) and Activity (excitement, loudness, speed). No per-font table is published as a dataset that I could find. (4) MyFonts tag dataset (Chen, Wang, Xu, Jin, Luo, ICCV 2019, Rochester and Adobe): 18,815 commercial MyFonts fonts with their user and foundry tags after cleaning (1,824 distinct tags, lower-cased, lemmatised, infrequent ones under 10 uses dropped), hundreds of thousands of font-tag pairs, an 80/10/10 split, and a mechanical-turk test set of 1,661 groups (3 fonts each, 3 workers) for the 300 most frequent tags. Tags are binary: they say a font matches, not how strongly. Downloadable as dataset.tar.gz from a Google Drive link on the project page; whether it holds font files, rendered images or only tag lists is not stated. (5) Its co-occurrence embeddings: a 2025 paper (arXiv 2508.18825) builds a tag graph from the same kind of data (17,380 fonts, 1,818 tags, 16.1 tags per font on average, median tag used by 35 fonts), weights edges with (P(i|j)+P(j|i))/2 and takes the 100 smallest Laplacian eigenvectors as 100-dimensional tag vectors. The vectors are the thesaurus idea in the brief, but no release statement is given and no nearest-neighbour list is printed.
provider_and_url: O'Donovan: https://www.dgp.toronto.edu/~donovan/font/ , paper https://www.dgp.toronto.edu/~donovan/font/fontSelection.pdf , supplemental https://www.dgp.toronto.edu/~donovan/font/supplemental.pdf , DOI https://doi.org/10.1145/2601097.2601110 . FontLex: https://aclanthology.org/L18-1010/ (PDF https://aclanthology.org/L18-1010.pdf), data page given in the paper http://gerard.demelo.org/fonts/ (did not load for me); Predicting Semantic Signatures of Fonts http://gerard.demelo.org/papers/font-attributes.pdf (not readable by my fetch tool); journal extension http://gerard.demelo.org/papers/typography-semantics.pdf (same). Shaikh 2006: https://soma.sbcc.edu/users/russotti/113/personality_Shaikh.pdf ; 2016 chapter abstract: https://portfolio.erau.edu/en/publications/perception-of-fonts-perceived-personality-traits-and-appropriate-/ . MyFonts dataset: https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/tchen45/font/font.html , paper https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ICCV_2019/papers/Chen_Large-Scale_Tag-Based_Font_Retrieval_With_Generative_Feature_Learning_ICCV_2019_paper.pdf (arXiv 1909.02072). Co-occurrence embeddings: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18825 . Related: Impression-CLIP https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16350 ; Hierarchical co-embedding of font shapes and impression tags https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04158 ; Font Impression Estimation in the Wild https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15236 . Stanford class project on inducing attributes from FontJoy embeddings: https://www.juliagong.com/docs/typefaces.pdf . Typographic Stroop with fast/slow ratings: Lewis and Walker 1989, https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1989.tb02317.x .
catalog_coverage: Not counted exactly, and the reason matters: counting needs the family names inside attribute.zip or gwfonts.zip, and downloading those needs your approval, so I did not. Bounds instead. O'Donovan and FontLex: at most 200 of 2,099 families (9.5%), and the real number is lower, because the 200 include web fonts from the Typekit blog seeds (the paper's own example is Gill Sans) and separate styles (a Stanford project lists 'Source Sans Pro Semibold' as one of the 200; it found only 161 of the 200 in the FontJoy list). By source: Google 1,760: some tens to at most 200; Fontshare 64: 0 (the service is from about 2020, the data from 2013 to 2014); Collletttivo 26 and Tunera 23: 0 (both founded after the data); Velvetyne 63 and Use & Modify 163: probably 0, not checked [uncertain]. Predicted-score extensions (kNN on CNN embeddings, 37 attributes): cover whatever the authors embedded (FontJoy's 1,861 fonts in the Stanford replication); I found no published file of those predictions. MyFonts dataset: 0 families directly, since these are commercial fonts and not ours. Its only use here is the vocabulary: measured by me, the 200 most frequent MyFonts tags (Table 3 of the paper's supplement, transcribed into scratchpad myfonts_top200.json) overlap our tag words as follows: 13 equal a Google Expressive or Theme tag name (art-deco, art-nouveau, blackletter, brush, cute, fancy, futuristic, happy, inline, playful, stencil, techno, vintage); Velvetyne 52 of its 159 distinct tags are among them, Collletttivo 34 of 73, Tunera 34 of 91, Use & Modify 15 of 45, Fontshare 22 of 53. Shaikh: 20 fonts (2006) and 40 typefaces (2016), mostly system fonts: effectively 0 of ours.
granularity: O'Donovan: per font style (Gill Sans and Gill Sans Light are separate fonts), continuous 0 to 100 per attribute for 31 attributes, binary for 6. FontLex: per word, a 200-vector over fonts. Shaikh: per font, mean of a 4-point scale per adjective pair. MyFonts: per family (the regular style is rendered), binary tags with no strength, ranking information only for the top 300 tags on 1,661 test groups. None gives italic or variable-axis detail.
signal_type: Semantic mood from human judgement, with shape words mixed in (thin, wide, angular, italic, monospace). MyFonts tags are free-form labels of genre, use, era and mood. Shaikh gives dimensions (Potency, Evaluative, Activity), not per-font labels.
mood_dimensions_covered: MOTION / ACTIVE (the case in the brief): (a) O'Donovan has no speed, active, energetic or fast attribute among its 31 + 6. The nearest are attention-grabbing, dramatic, strong, sharp, angular and italic. Their rater-agreement scores (share of raters' answers predicted by the fitted values, supplemental table, average over 31 = 69.52%) are strong 84.80%, dramatic 71.08%, attention-grabbing 69.23%, angular 62.80%, sharp 62.02%: the shape-like words that matter for speed are among the least agreed. (b) Shaikh and Chaparro 2016 name the construct: Activity = excitement, loudness and speed. It supports using Google's Excited, Loud and Active together as one axis, but it ships no per-font scores. (c) Lewis and Walker 1989 pretested typefaces on fast-slow and heavy-light and found raters agreed; Palatino Italic scored fast, Cooper Black slow (as summarised in a search result, original not read) [uncertain]. (d) MyFonts top-200 tags include dynamic, sport, lively, bouncy, wild, crazy, game, movie, urban and italic. 'speed', 'fast' and 'racing' are not in the top 200; the tail of the 1,824 is not visible without the data [uncertain]. LOUD: O'Donovan attention-grabbing, dramatic, strong; MyFonts bold, heavy, fat, poster, headline, wild, crazy. CALM: O'Donovan calm (70.80%), gentle (66.19%), soft (75.86%); MyFonts soft, clean, simple, minimal, neutral. FUTURISTIC / TECHNO: O'Donovan technical (62.94%) and modern (65.86%); MyFonts futuristic, techno, technical, computer, mechanical, modular, industrial, minimal; the co-occurrence paper notes 'technological', 'wide', 'extend' and 'square' cluster together. ELEGANT: O'Donovan graceful (65.05%), delicate (63.83%), formal (69.44%), attractive; MyFonts elegant (the 11th most frequent tag), fashion, feminine, graceful, romantic, stylish. Shaikh 2006: scripts rated more elegant. HANDMADE: O'Donovan sloppy (70.20%), clumsy (70.14%), disorderly (73.88%), artistic (73.80%), cursive (binary); MyFonts handwrite, handmade, hand-drawn, sketch, brush, rough, grunge. Net: good vocabulary for calm, elegant, handmade, techno and loud; thin for speed, which only appears as dynamic, sport, lively and italic.
query_style_specificity: Helps more for loose and broad requests than for tight ones. The crowd attributes agree most on concrete axes (thin 93.16%, strong 84.80%, wide 81.11%, soft 75.86%) and least on mood words (friendly 64.39%, warm 64.53%, angular 62.80%, sharp 62.02%), so a tight request like 'fast' has no matching attribute and the nearest words are noisy. The MyFonts tags are strong for genre and use (script, stencil, blackletter, poster, logo) and carry a few tight moods (futuristic, techno, dynamic).
quality_evidence: No dataset here was evaluated on 'fast' or 'action' queries; everything below is indirect. O'Donovan 2014: fitted attribute values predict held-out rater answers 69.52% on average over the 31 relative attributes; the learned similarity metric predicts 75.83% of held-out rater answers against an oracle bound of 80.79% (Table 1); gradient-boosted trees predict the attributes from font outlines with mean absolute error 8.51 on the 0-100 scale versus 10.76 for LASSO (leave-one-out). In the authors' studies, either new interface made users three times more likely to find a target font than the baseline list, but the attribute interface did not beat the baseline on mean distance to the target (effect size 0.07, not significant); in person, participants significantly preferred the attribute interface to the baseline. The authors report large disagreement between raters. FontLex 2018: for 8 of 10 emotions raters (30 per task, mechanical turk) clearly preferred the fonts the data called congruent; for most of 25 randomly sampled words, fonts with strong associations were preferred, and for all but 2 of the words fonts with weak associations were dispreferred; kNN-extended scores have about 9% mean absolute error. Chen 2019: a plain tag-recognition model already beat joint-embedding retrieval models, and the full model reached mAP 28.08 and nDCG 70.04 on the first query set against 26.29 and 68.67 without the three modules (Table 1; which query set is the first is my reading) [uncertain]; the authors say tags 'collected from the web are inevitably noisy and incomplete' and that a joint text embedding fits font tags poorly. Co-occurrence embedding 2025: its tag vectors beat BERT and CLIP text vectors on a consistency test (overlap coefficient 0.344 versus 0.175 for CLIP and 0.091 for BERT, low-frequency tags), which says general word embeddings misjudge which impression words go together on fonts. Our own measurement: the vocabulary-overlap counts under catalog_coverage.
known_noise: O'Donovan: raters agree 69.52% on average, 62% on the worst; the paper rejects about 8.1% of tasks (supplemental says 9.11%); the same font's attribute is an average over 64 answers (8 workers x 8 pairs). Predicted attributes for the other 1,078 fonts add model error (MAE 8.51 of 100). FontLex: kNN extension error about 9%; word-font links depend on the emotion lexicon, and no arousal or speed axis exists in its ten emotions. MyFonts: tags typed by foundries, designers and users; missing tags are common (a font can be a match without the tag); tags per font run 1 to 184 (mean 16.1); the median tag is used by only 35 fonts, so most tags are sparse. Shaikh: 20 to 40 fonts, convenience samples, a 4-point scale.
name_and_memory_bias: The labels themselves are low on name bias: O'Donovan removed font names from the rating interface and used one neutral word ('handgloves'), and Chen rendered random character strings. Using them through an LLM brings the name problem back: the model knows popular Google fonts and will answer from memory, which the current prompt already fights with its 'very common' rule. Imported vocabularies do not change that; only a per-font signal does.
untagged_rows: As per-font labels they leave about 90% or more of the catalog uncovered (at most 200 fonts), and the ones left uncovered are exactly the indie and Fontshare rows. As a vocabulary (a thesaurus) nothing is left untagged, because it works on the request side. A per-font use would need transfer from tagged neighbours (the FontLex and Stanford kNN approach, or the exemplar method in 'Font Impression Estimation in the Wild', which ensembles the impressions of similar fonts).
text_interference_risk: Not applicable to using the vocabulary. For the data itself: O'Donovan and Chen showed neutral strings so word meaning would not sway raters. If we later render text for a visual method, use the same neutral approach (a separate item).
integration_path: Three ways, in order of value for money. (A) Vocabulary only (recommended). Build a small thesaurus file offline, server/data/vibe-thesaurus.json, format { "fast": { "also": ["speed", "dynamic", "sporty", "lively"], "tags": ["Active", "Excited", "Loud", "Futuristic", "Techno"], "shape": ["italic", "slanted", "condensed", "angular", "sharp", "heavy"], "against": ["Calm", "Stiff"] }, ... }, seeded from O'Donovan's 31 attribute names, the MyFonts top-200 tags and Shaikh's Activity words (excitement, loudness, speed), written by a model in one batch and reviewed by a person. At search time, plain code finds thesaurus words in the request and (i) adds a short 'read this as' line to the user part of the prompt (keeps the cached system prompt unchanged), and optionally (ii) scores catalog rows by overlap with the 'tags' and 'shape' lists to shortlist before the model. (B) Small calibration set. Join the 200 O'Donovan fonts to the catalog by family name (needs attribute.zip, with your approval), then compare crowd 'attention-grabbing', 'dramatic', 'strong', 'sharp' with Google's Active, Loud, Excited and with measured slant and weight. Output: a CSV (family, attribute, value) under scripts/ and a printed correlation table. It checks whether Google's tags agree with humans on the overlap; it does not label new fonts. (C) Co-occurrence thesaurus from the MyFonts data. Only if dataset.tar.gz contains per-font tag lists (unverified): compute the (P(i|j)+P(j|i))/2 graph, 100-dimensional spectral vectors, and write the 10 nearest tags for each of the 1,824 tags to server/data/tag-neighbours.json as { tag: [[neighbour, score], ...] }. Do this only if (A) proves too weak.
tokens_per_row: Zero per row for all three. Option A adds about 300 to 800 tokens once to the instructions, or a few dozen tokens per search in the user prompt (not cacheable, but tiny). The catalog text stays as it is (about 45,000 tokens by my estimate).
vocabulary_alignment: Adds new terms, with partial overlap. Measured by me: of O'Donovan's 31 relative attributes, 6 equal a Google tag name (artistic, playful, calm, formal, modern, happy) and 4 equal an Expressive tag (artistic, playful, calm, happy); of the MyFonts top 200, 13 equal a Google Expressive or Theme name and 19 equal any Google tag name (adding formal, geometric, grotesque, humanist, informal, modern). Shaikh's Activity (excitement, loudness, speed) has no single Google word but maps onto Excited, Loud and Active as a group. A thesaurus is the bridge that makes the extra terms usable.
explainability: Yes, but only through the vocabulary: a result can say it matched because the request word 'fast' expands to italic, condensed, sporty, Active, and quote the row's tags. Per-font crowd scores (for example 'rated 82 of 100 attention-grabbing') exist for at most 200 fonts.
determinism: The data and a stored thesaurus are fixed, so expansion and shortlist scoring are deterministic. The model stage is not.
build_effort: Option A: about 1 day for an agent: a batch script that asks a model to draft about 150 request words, a validator (every tag named must exist in the catalog vocabulary), the one-function expansion in server/vibe.ts, a unit test, a 20-query smoke run. Option B: about half a day after the download is approved. Option C: 1 to 2 days, mostly figuring out the tarball's contents.
per_search_cost_and_latency: A and B add none (dictionary lookup, milliseconds). C adds none at search time if precomputed.
one_off_cost: A: one batch of model calls on the subscription (minutes). B: attribute.zip, size not stated, small. C: dataset.tar.gz on Google Drive, size not stated, probably large if it holds images. I downloaded none of them.
human_effort: A: about 1 to 2 hours to review the expansions of the 40 to 60 most likely request words (a person should check each 'shape' list), then minutes per new word. B and C: none.
asset_access: O'Donovan: plain files on the University of Toronto project page (attribute.zip, similarity.zip, gwfonts.zip); I did not check that site's robots.txt and did not download [uncertain]. MyFonts dataset: a Google Drive link on the Rochester page; the page says to ask the authors with questions. FontLex: the paper points to gerard.demelo.org/fonts, which did not load for me, so availability is unverified. Shaikh: PDFs only. The 2025 co-occurrence paper: no code or data statement found. Several PDFs could be read only through my fetch tool's saved copies converted with pdftotext.
licence_and_provenance: No licence is stated for the O'Donovan files, the MyFonts dataset, the FontLex lexicon data or the Shaikh results. The LREC paper text is under CC BY 4.0 (ACL Anthology notice for post-2016 papers), which covers the paper, not necessarily the data [uncertain]. The MyFonts fonts are commercial and the tags are user and foundry content, so redistributing derived data inside a shipped product needs checking; using a few vocabulary words is safe. The O'Donovan gwfonts files are Google fonts of 2013 (OFL or Apache) mixed with Typekit-sourced web fonts that are not free, so do not reuse those files.
etiquette: No scraping needed; fetch the project pages once. Never velvetyne.fr. Do not hammer the Google Drive link. Semantic Scholar's API answered HTTP 429 once and I did not retry.
maintenance_and_freshness: All static: 2013 to 2014 (O'Donovan), 2006 and 2016 (Shaikh), 2018 (FontLex), 2019 (MyFonts). Google Fonts grew from 822 families in October 2017 (FontLex paper) to our 1,760 now, so none covers current fonts. The vocabulary ages slowly. Research continues (2024 to 2026 papers on MyFonts-based embeddings) but publishes no updated data. Keeping a thesaurus current is a rare edit, not a pipeline.
risks_and_limitations: The brief's premise partly fails: there is no 'fast' attribute and no released thesaurus. The '37 crowd attributes' are 31 crowd plus 6 hand-labelled, on 200 fonts; FontLex has 200 fonts, not 2,000; the 2006 Shaikh paper found five font families, and the Activity factor is from the 2016 chapter. The MyFonts dataset is commercial fonts, so it cannot label our fonts, and its co-occurrence vectors are published as method only. Data are 7 to 19 years old. Adding an LLM-written thesaurus risks echoing the model's own bias, which is why a person must review the shape lists. A thesaurus helps requests whose words appear in it and does nothing for fonts whose rows carry no matching tag.
evaluation_hook: Held-out check: hide the Google Active, Loud, Excited and Futuristic tags on a random 20% of Google rows, run the thesaurus expansion plus tag scoring over the rest, and measure recall of the hidden ones in the top 50 for the requests 'fast', 'loud', 'techno'. Then have a person rate result grids for 20 to 30 requests with and without the expansion. If attribute.zip is approved, add the correlation table from Option B.
recommendation_for_font_explorer: Use partly: take the words, not the data. (1) Build the thesaurus (Option A) from O'Donovan's attribute names, the MyFonts top-200 tags and Shaikh's Activity words; for 'fast' include italic, slanted, condensed, angular, sharp and heavy as shape words, and dynamic, sporty, lively, Active, Excited, Loud as mood words. (2) Do not build per-font scoring from these datasets: at most 200 fonts are labelled and none of the 339 non-Google rows. (3) Skip the MyFonts co-occurrence route unless a quick look at the tarball (with your approval to download it) shows per-font tag lists; the thesaurus can be drafted by a model in the meantime. (4) Treat O'Donovan as a small human check on Google's Active, Loud and Excited tags (Option B), not as a feature. Where it sits: it is the cheapest item (no new per-font data, no tokens per row) and it only fixes the request side; the font side still needs measured traits, vision labels or tag transfer for the 339 rows (items measured-traits, vision-labels, indie-gap). Smallest first step: write the thesaurus entries for ten request words (fast, action, loud, calm, techno, elegant, handmade, playful, heavy, retro), wire the 'read this as' line into the user prompt, and compare 'fast movement or action' results before and after.
